summary: Describes the Media Gateway Control Protocol, an interface and protocol used between parts of a decomposed multimedia gateway. A Call Agent holds the call control logic while media gateways handle conversion such as TDM voice to voice over IP, and the Call Agent controls the gateway's endpoints. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A phone-call bridge can be split into a brain and a set of hands. MGCP is how the brain tells the hands what to connect and when.

subtitle: How a Call Agent 'brain' tells telephony gateways to create, change and tear down voice connections over UDP.

tldr.problem: Phone networks carry audio on circuits and the Internet carries it in packets, so something must convert between them. Putting all the call logic inside every conversion box makes the boxes complicated.
tldr.mechanism: MGCP splits the system in two. A Call Agent holds the call control intelligence and sends text commands over UDP to media gateways, which own endpoints and create, modify and delete connections on them. Gateways report events such as off-hook back to the Call Agent.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 2705 and is updated by RFC 3661. The IESG note points implementers to RFC 3015 as the standards-based way to meet the same needs.

today: RFC 3435 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 2705 and is updated by RFC 3661. Its IESG note says the IETF and ITU-T consider RFC 3015 the standards-based way, including reviewed security considerations, to meet the needs MGCP was designed to address.

sections.title: Splitting Call Control from Media
sections.content:
RFC 3435 describes an abstract programming interface (MGCI) and a protocol (MGCP, version 1.0) for controlling media gateways from external call control elements called Call Agents. A media gateway converts between the audio on telephone circuits and the data packets carried over the Internet or other packet networks.

The RFC lists several kinds of gateway: trunking gateways, Voice over ATM gateways, residential gateways (an analog RJ11 line to a Voice over IP network), access gateways, business gateways, Network Access Servers, and circuit or packet switches that offer a control interface.

MGCP is, in the RFC's own words, essentially a master/slave protocol: the gateways execute commands sent by the Call Agents. The document therefore specifies gateway behavior in great detail and only those parts of a Call Agent, such as timer management, that are needed for the protocol to work. It does not define how several Call Agents synchronize with each other, and if they do not send coherent commands, inconsistent behavior should be expected.

The IESG note says the document describes a protocol that is being deployed in a number of products, and that implementers should be aware of RFC 3015, which the IETF and ITU-T consider the standards-based way to meet the needs MGCP was designed for.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone company box that turns phone-line sound into Internet packets does not need to know how to run a whole call. MGCP lets a separate boss do the thinking and the box just do what it is told.

sections.title: Endpoints, Connections and Calls
sections.content:
MGCP assumes a connection model built from endpoints and connections. Endpoints are sources and sinks of data and can be physical (a trunk interface or an analog phone line) or virtual (an audio source in an announcement server). Connections can be point to point or multipoint, and can run over RTP and UDP on an IP network, over AAL2 on an ATM network, or over an internal path such as a TDM backplane, as in a hairpin connection.

The RFC isolates these endpoint types: digital channel (DS0), analog line, announcement server access point, Interactive Voice Response access point, conference bridge access point, packet relay and ATM trunk side interface. It states that the list is not final and that gateways are free to mix types in one product.

Connections are grouped into calls, but the call identifier has little semantic meaning to MGCP and is mainly kept for backwards compatibility and for accounting or management. Call identifiers are hexadecimal strings created by the Call Agent, at most 32 characters long. Connection identifiers are created by the gateway, are also hexadecimal strings of at most 32 characters, and must not be reused on the same endpoint within at least 3 minutes.

For each connection the Call Agent gives the gateway local directives (mode, preferred codecs, packetization, echo cancellation and so on) and, when available, the remote session description from the other end. The gateway then picks the resources and replies with its own session description, written in SDP (RFC 2327).
sections.plainLanguage: An endpoint is like one phone socket on a wall, and a connection is a wire from that socket to another. A call is just a label that says which wires belong to the same chat.

sections.title: Naming Endpoints and Call Agents
sections.content:
An endpoint name has two case-insensitive parts: a local name and the domain name of the gateway that manages it, written local-endpoint-name@domain-name. The local name is hierarchical, with terms separated by a single slash, and the least specific term on the left. An example from the RFC is hrd4/56@gw23.example.net.

Two wildcards select endpoints. An asterisk means all values of a term known to the gateway, whatever their service state, and a dollar sign means any one value, normally an in-service endpoint. It is recommended to wildcard only from the right, and mixing the two is discouraged as error prone.

Call Agents are named the same way, for example ca1@ca.whatever.net. Entities are identified by domain name rather than IP address so that DNS can supply several addresses and fail-over is possible; implementations must retry another address if one cannot be reached.

Each endpoint has exactly one notified entity, the Call Agent it currently sends commands to. It starts as a provisioned value and changes only when a command carries a new NotifiedEntity parameter (or on a warm or cold restart). Any Call Agent may still send commands to the endpoint, which is why the security section matters. If no port is given, the default Call Agent port 2727 is used.
sections.plainLanguage: Every socket has an address like a street number plus a town name. A star in the address means every house on the street, and a dollar sign means just pick any one house.

sections.title: The Nine Commands
sections.content:
MGCP has nine commands, split between connection handling and endpoint handling. Every command is acknowledged with a response carrying a return code.

  • EndpointConfiguration tells the gateway the coding (A-law or mu-law) expected on the line side of an endpoint.
  • NotificationRequest asks the gateway to watch for events, such as off-hook or DTMF digits, and to apply signals, such as ringing.
  • Notify is the gateway's report that requested events happened.
  • CreateConnection, ModifyConnection and DeleteConnection manage connections. A gateway may also send DeleteConnection to say a connection can no longer be sustained.
  • AuditEndpoint and AuditConnection let the Call Agent read the state of an endpoint or connection.
  • RestartInProgress lets the gateway say that endpoints are going out of service or coming back.

A NotificationRequest lists RequestedEvents and, for each event, one or more actions: notify immediately, swap audio, accumulate, accumulate according to a digit map, keep signals active, process an embedded NotificationRequest, or ignore. Notify, Accumulate, Keep Signal(s) Active, Embedded NotificationRequest and Ignore are required. Time-out signals such as ringing stop as soon as a requested event is detected, unless the Keep Signals Active action says otherwise.

The creation, modification and deletion commands can carry an encapsulated NotificationRequest that shares their fate: both are accepted or both are refused. For example, one CreateConnection can prepare a connection, start ringing and ask to be told about the off-hook event, and the phone must not ring if the connection cannot be set up.
sections.plainLanguage: There are nine kinds of message. The boss can say connect this, change that, hang up, tell me when the phone is picked up, or how are you doing. The hands can say something happened, or I am going offline.

sections.title: Setting Up Connections and Choosing Modes
sections.content:
When both endpoints sit on gateways run by the same Call Agent, the RFC describes three steps. The Call Agent asks the first gateway to create a connection and gets back a session description (IP address, UDP port, codec parameters). It then asks the second gateway to create its connection, passing in the first description, and gets the second gateway's own description. Finally a ModifyConnection hands that second description to the first endpoint, after which media flows both ways. If the Call Agents differ, they synchronize through a Call Agent to Call Agent protocol such as SIP.

When both endpoints are on the same gateway, a single CreateConnection can name a second endpoint instead of a remote session description. That really creates two connections, and the second one starts in send/receive mode.

Each connection has a mode: send only, receive only, send/receive, conference, inactive, loopback, continuity test, network loopback or network continuity test. The send and receive modes control which direction media flows. Conference mode also forwards media from one conference connection to the others. Loopback and continuity test modes support trunk circuit maintenance, and the network variants echo or process packets arriving from the connection.

A gateway that has exported a local descriptor but not yet received a remote one must pick a safe behavior. In receive only mode it accepts the media and passes it to the endpoint. In inactive, loopback or continuity test mode it must not pass the media through. Modes that need a remote descriptor, such as send/receive, are rejected with error 527.

DeleteConnection returns statistics for Internet media streams: packets and octets sent and received, packets lost, interarrival jitter and average transmission delay.
sections.plainLanguage: To connect two people, the boss gets a phone number from the first helper, gives it to the second helper, then gets the second helper's number and gives that back to the first. After that they can talk to each other directly.

sections.title: Events, Signals, Digit Maps and Packages
sections.content:
Events are things an endpoint can detect, such as off-hook. Signals are things it can apply, such as dial tone or ringing. Both are grouped in packages, and a name looks like package-name/event, for example L/dl. An event or signal on a connection adds the connection id after an at sign, as in G/rt@0A3F58. Packages are the preferred way to extend MGCP: a package can define events, signals, actions, extra connection modes, local connection options, restart methods, reason codes and more. Package names that start with x- are for experiments and are never registered.

Signals come in three types. On/off signals last until explicitly turned off. Time-out signals last until cancelled or a signal-specific period passes, then raise an operation complete event. Brief signals are short enough to stop by themselves.

Collecting dialed numbers one digit at a time would cause many interactions, so the Call Agent loads the gateway with a digit map, a pattern in a syntax derived from the Unix egrep command. For example (xxxxxxx|x11) with a current dial string of 41 becomes 411 on the next digit. That is a complete match for x11, so the gateway reports it. Gateways are recommended to support digit maps of at least 2048 bytes per endpoint.

Events detected while a Notify is being delivered go into a FIFO quarantine buffer. The QuarantineHandling parameter says whether quarantined events are processed or discarded, and whether the gateway may send one notification (step by step) or several (loop).
sections.plainLanguage: Packages are like toolboxes of extra tricks, each with a name. A digit map is a list of phone-number shapes, so the helper knows when you have finished dialing and can tell the boss the whole number at once.

sections.title: The Text Message Format
sections.content:
MGCP messages are lines of text separated by carriage return and line feed (or just a line feed). A command has a command line followed by parameter lines, then optionally an empty line and a session description in SDP. The grammar is given in ABNF in Appendix A and is case-insensitive except for the SDP part.

The command line has four items separated by white space: the four-letter verb, the transaction identifier, the endpoint name and the protocol version, written MGCP 1.0. The transaction identifier is a number from 1 to 999,999,999 and a response repeats it so it can be matched to the command. An entity must not reuse an identifier within three minutes of the previous command that used it finishing. Experimental verbs start with the letter X.

Parameter lines are a short code, a colon and a value, for example C: for CallId, I: for ConnectionId, M: for the mode, L: for LocalConnectionOptions and N: for NotifiedEntity.

Every response starts with a three-digit return code. The ranges are: 000 to 099 response acknowledgement, 100 to 199 provisional, 200 to 299 success, 400 to 499 transient error (a later similar request may succeed) and 500 to 599 permanent error. Codes 800 to 899 are package specific. Examples are 200 (executed normally), 250 (connection deleted), 401 (phone already off hook), 410 (no endpoint available), 518 (unsupported package) and 527 (missing RemoteConnectionDescriptor).
sections.plainLanguage: Messages are plain notes written in words, with a short code word at the start saying what to do. Replies start with a number, like grades: a 2 means all fine, a 4 means try again later, a 5 means it will never work.

sections.title: Reliable Delivery over UDP
sections.content:
MGCP runs over UDP. Unless a port is given, Call Agents send to the default gateway port 2427 and gateways send to the default Call Agent port 2727. Responses go back to the source address of the command.

Since UDP can lose packets and most commands are not idempotent (running a CreateConnection twice would corrupt state), the protocol must provide at-most-once execution. Entities remember responses to recent transactions for a timer called T-HIST, suggested at 30 seconds. A repeated command with a known transaction identifier gets the stored response resent instead of being executed again, and a command still being executed gets a provisional response.

The RFC deliberately gives no fixed retransmission timer, but requires at least exponential backoff, with the maximum timer suggested at 4 seconds (RTO-MAX). After each retransmission the delay estimate is doubled and a random value is chosen between half of it and all of it, so repeated traffic slows down under congestion and notifications triggered by one event do not synchronize.

Long-running transactions send a provisional response (code 100, or 101 if queued) and the sender switches to a longer timer, LONGTRAN-TIMER, default 5 seconds. A final response that followed a provisional one should be acknowledged by a Response Acknowledgement (return code 000), forming a three-way handshake.

Implementations must accept MGCP datagrams of at least 4000 bytes, relying on IP fragmentation. Several messages can be put in one datagram, separated by a line with a single dot, to keep their order or share fate.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail sometimes gets lost, so if no answer comes you ask again, waiting a bit longer each time. The helper keeps a note of what it already did, so asking twice never makes it do the same thing twice.

sections.title: Failover, Restarts and Race Conditions
sections.content:
Because an endpoint talks to its notified entity by domain name, a backup Call Agent can take over by sending the endpoints a new NotifiedEntity. The RFC says plainly that there is no handover conflict resolution between Call Agents: it relies on them knowing what they are doing and communicating with each other. AuditEndpoint can be used to learn the current notified entity.

If a command goes unanswered after repeated retransmissions, the sender suspects a problem at a lower threshold (Max1) and treats the peer as disconnected at a higher one (Max2). A gateway that cannot reach its Call Agent becomes disconnected and follows the disconnected procedure, sending RestartInProgress with the disconnected method.

RestartInProgress carries a restart method: graceful (taken out of service after a delay, existing connections not yet affected), forced (taken out of service abruptly), restart (service restored in a clean state), disconnected and cancel-graceful.

Race conditions are handled by the quarantine list described earlier, by explicit rules for the order of commands, and by transactional semantics. For example, a running CreateConnection or ModifyConnection is cancelled when a DeleteConnection arrives for the endpoint, and the cancelled transaction still gets a final response, with error 407 recommended. The RFC also includes sections on avoiding a restart avalanche and on load control.
sections.plainLanguage: If the boss's phone line goes dead, a backup boss can call the helpers and say I am in charge now. When a helper has to switch off, it announces whether it is leaving right now or after finishing its current jobs.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
Any entity can send a command to an MGCP endpoint, so without protection an attacker could set up unauthorized calls or interfere with real ones. The RFC expects MGCP messages to always be carried over secure Internet connections using the IP security architecture, with either the IP Authentication Header or the IP Encapsulating Security Payload (RFC 2401, RFC 2402, RFC 2406). Gateways and Call Agents should accept only messages for which IP security provided authentication. Encryption adds protection against eavesdropping, and is also requested if session descriptions carry session keys.

These measures do not necessarily stop denial of service by a misbehaving gateway or Call Agent, but they identify it so that its authorization can be withdrawn.

For media, the Call Agent can give gateways session keys to encrypt audio. The RFC names uncontrolled barge-in: someone sends media packets to the address and port of a connection and the signals are played on the line side. Accepting packets only from known sources helps but slows call setup and can be fooled by source spoofing. Encrypting and authenticating packets with a key conveyed at setup avoids the delay and protects strongly against address spoofing.

Section 8 of the RFC, Security Considerations, simply refers back to this section.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone could shout orders at a helper, so the messages need a secret handshake that proves who sent them. The talking itself can also be scrambled so nobody can listen in or butt into the call.

items.desc: Tear down a connection and collect statistics.

items.desc: Ask the gateway to watch for events and apply signals.

items.desc: Read the state of an endpoint.

items.label: AuditConnection
items.desc: Read the parameters of a connection.

items.label: RestartInProgress
items.desc: Gateway signals endpoints going in or out of service.

items.label: Response acknowledgement
items.desc: Confirms receipt of a final response.

items.label: Provisional response
items.desc: Transaction is still being executed or is queued.

items.label: Transient error
items.desc: A later similar request may be honored.

items.label: Permanent error
items.desc: A condition that will not disappear with time.

items.title: On/off (OO)
items.text: Lasts until explicitly turned off or the endpoint restarts. Repeated requests are valid and not errors.

items.title: Time-out (TO)
items.text: Lasts until cancelled or a signal-specific time passes, then raises an operation complete event.

items.title: Brief (BR)
items.text: Short enough to stop on its own, such as a DTMF digit.
